title: Introduction to NLP
summary: Natural Language Processing is teaching computers to work with human language, the core of GenAI. Before deep models, text was turned into numbers using techniques like TF-IDF. Learning these classical methods builds intuition for how machines repres
content:
# Introduction to NLP ##### The word that appeared in every single document A legal-tech team in Hyderabad built a system to route incoming contracts to the right specialist — employment, property, IP, or commercial. They vectorised 8,000 contracts with a simple word-count approach, trained a classifier, and got 61% accuracy across four classes. Barely better than guessing at two of them. Someone printed the top 30 features by weight. The list read: *the, of, and, to, in, shall, hereby, agreement, party, whereas, herein, thereof...* Every one of those words appears in every contract ever written. The model had spent all its capacity on vocabulary that carries zero discriminative information, and the words that actually mattered — *lease*, *severance*, *trademark*, *indemnify* — were buried under legal boilerplate that swamped them by sheer frequency. They switched from raw counts to TF-IDF. Accuracy went to 87%. One line of code. TF-IDF's insight, formalised by Karen Spärck Jones in 1972, is beautifully simple: **a word is informative in proportion to how rare it is across your corpus.** "Shall" appears in all 8,000 contracts and tells you nothing. "Trademark" appears in 340 and tells you almost everything. You will not use TF-IDF for most GenAI work. But you will use it more often than you expect — it is still the backbone of keyword search, it is the "sparse" half of hybrid retrieval in production RAG systems, and understanding it builds the intuition you need for embeddings tomorrow. ##### The NLP task landscape Before the techniques, a map of what NLP does: | Task | Input → Output | Example | |---|---|---| | **Classification** | Text → label | Spam, sentiment, contract type | | **Named entity recognition** | Text → spans + types | Find PAN numbers, company names, dates | | **Sequence labelling** | Text → per-token label | Part-of-speech tagging | | **Question answering** | Question + context → answer span | "What is the notice period?" | | **Summarisation** | Long text → short text | Contract → key terms | | **Translation** | Text (L1) → text (L2) | Hindi → English | | **Generation** | Prompt → continuation | Everything an LLM does | | **Retrieval** | Query → ranked documents | Semantic search, RAG | Today covers the classical pipeline for the first of these, and the preprocessing that feeds all of them. ##### Tokenization A computer cannot process "the quick brown fox." It processes numbers. **Tokenization** is the first step: splitting text into units. The naive approach: ```python text = "Dr. Sharma's clinic in Pune isn't open on 2nd Oct. Call +91-98200-11223!" print(text.split()) # ['Dr.', "Sharma's", 'clinic', 'in', 'Pune', "isn't", 'open', 'on', '2nd', # 'Oct.', 'Call', '+91-98200-11223!'] ``` Immediately problematic. `Oct.` carries a period. `isn't` should probably be two tokens. The phone number has a trailing exclamation mark glued on. A real tokenizer handles this: ```python import spacy nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_sm") doc = nlp(text) for token in doc[:12]: print(f"{token.text:18s} {token.lemma_:14s} {token.pos_:8s} " f"stop={token.is_stop!s:5s} punct={token.is_punct}") ``` spaCy splits `isn't` into `is` + `n't`, keeps `Dr.` intact as an abbreviation, and recognises the phone number pattern. **Three levels of tokenization**, worth knowing because they matter later: - **Word-level** — intuitive, but the vocabulary explodes (English has hundreds of thousands of forms) and unseen words become ``. - **Character-level** — tiny vocabulary, no unknown words, but sequences get very long and each token carries little meaning. - **Subword** — the modern answer. Break rare words into pieces: `unhappiness` → `un` + `happi` + `ness`. Fixed vocabulary of ~30,000–100,000, no unknown words ever, and morphologically related words share pieces. Every LLM you will use employs subword tokenization (BPE, WordPiece, or SentencePiece). A practical consequence for Indian languages: English text averages about 4 characters per token, while Hindi or Tamil in Devanagari/Tamil script often runs 1–2 characters per token — so the *same content* can cost 3–4× more tokens, and therefore 3–4× more money, in an LLM API call. ##### Stopwords, stemming, lemmatization **Stopwords** are extremely common words — *the, is, at, which, on*. They carry grammatical structure but little topical meaning. ```python from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import ENGLISH_STOP_WORDS print(len(ENGLISH_STOP_WORDS)) # 318 ``` Remove them for keyword-based tasks. **Do not remove them for sentiment or for anything an LLM will read** — "not" is a stopword in many lists, and removing it inverts your meaning. The Kochi sentiment failure from Day 18 has a cousin here, caused by a one-line `remove_stopwords()` call. **Stemming** chops suffixes with crude rules. Fast, sometimes nonsensical. ```python from nltk.stem import PorterStemmer stemmer = PorterStemmer() for w in ["running", "runs", "ran", "studies", "university", "universe"]: print(f"{w:12s} -> {stemmer.stem(w)}") # running -> run # runs -> run # ran -> ran ← missed; not a suffix rule # studies -> studi ← not a word # university-> univers ← collides with 'universe'! ``` **Lemmatization** reduces to the dictionary form using vocabulary and grammar. Slower, correct. ```python for token in nlp("running runs ran studies better mice"): print(f"{token.text:10s} -> {token.lemma_}") # running -> run # runs -> run # ran -> run ← handled # studies -> study # better -> well # mice -> mouse ``` Use lemmatization when quality matters; stemming when you are processing millions of documents and speed dominates. ##### Bag of words The simplest text-to-numbers conversion: count how often each vocabulary word appears, ignore word order entirely. ```python from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer docs = [ "the food was good and the service was quick", "the food was not good the service was slow", "great ambience great food great service", ] cv = CountVectorizer() X = cv.fit_transform(docs) import pandas as pd print(pd.DataFrame(X.toarray(), columns=cv.get_feature_names_out())) ``` ``` ambience and food good great not quick service slow the was 0 0 1 1 1 0 0 1 1 0 2 2 1 0 0 1 1 0 1 0 1 1 2 2 2 1 0 1 0 3 0 0 1 0 0 0 ``` Two things are immediately visible. **`the` and `was` dominate** — the Hyderabad problem. And **documents 0 and 1 have nearly identical vectors** despite meaning opposite things, because bag-of-words discards order and treats `not` as just one more count. That is the fundamental limitation: **"dog bites man" and "man bites dog" produce identical vectors.** ##### TF-IDF TF-IDF weights each word by how frequent it is *in this document* and how rare it is *across the corpus*. $$\text{TF-IDF}(t, d) = \underbrace{\frac{\text{count}(t, d)}{\text{total terms in } d}}_{\text{term frequency}} \times \underbrace{\log\frac{N}{1 + \text{df}(t)}}_{\text{inverse document frequency}}$$ The IDF term is the whole idea. A word in all $N$ documents gets $\log(N/N) \approx 0$ — killed. A word in 1% of documents gets $\log(100) \approx 4.6$ — amplified. ```python from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer tfidf = TfidfVectorizer( lowercase=True, stop_words="english", ngram_range=(1, 2), # unigrams and bigrams min_df=2, # ignore terms in fewer than 2 documents max_df=0.85, # ignore terms in >85% of documents sublinear_tf=True, # use 1 + log(tf) — dampens repetition max_features=50_000, ) X = tfidf.fit_transform(corpus) print(X.shape, f"sparsity {1 - X.nnz / (X.shape[0] * X.shape[1]):.4%}") ``` Every argument there is doing real work: - **`min_df=2`** removes typos and one-off words that cannot generalise. - **`max_df=0.85`** removes corpus-wide boilerplate — a second line of defence past stopword removal, and the one that would have caught "shall" and "hereby." - **`sublinear_tf=True`** means a word appearing 100 times is not 100× more important than one appearing once. - **`ngram_range=(1,2)`** is the partial fix for word order, discussed next. TF-IDF vectors are **sparse** — a 50,000-word vocabulary with 200 words per document means 99.6% zeros. `scipy.sparse` stores only the non-zeros, which is why this scales to millions of documents on a laptop. ##### N-grams An n-gram is a contiguous sequence of n tokens. They recover *some* word order. ```python from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer text = ["the food was not good"] for n in [1, 2, 3]: v = CountVectorizer(ngram_range=(n, n)).fit(text) print(f"{n}-grams:", list(v.get_feature_names_out())) # 1-grams: ['food', 'good', 'not', 'the', 'was'] # 2-grams: ['food was', 'the food', 'was not', 'not good'] # 3-grams: ['the food was', 'food was not', 'was not good'] ``` **`not good` as a single bigram feature is the fix for the negation problem.** The classifier can now learn that this specific pair signals negative sentiment, which unigrams could never express. The cost is vocabulary explosion. Unigrams might give 20,000 features; adding bigrams can push it past 500,000. `min_df` is what keeps this manageable. **Practical guidance:** `ngram_range=(1, 2)` is the sweet spot for most classification. Trigrams rarely help and triple your feature count. ##### Text classification end to end ```python from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score from sklearn.metrics import classification_report import numpy as np X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split( texts, labels, test_size=0.2, stratify=labels, random_state=42 ) clf = Pipeline([ ("tfidf", TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english", ngram_range=(1, 2), min_df=2, max_df=0.9, sublinear_tf=True)), ("model", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, C=4.0, class_weight="balanced")), ]) scores = cross_val_score(clf, X_train, y_train, cv=5, scoring="f1_macro") print(f"CV F1: {scores.mean():.3f} ± {scores.std():.3f}") clf.fit(X_train, y_train) print(classification_report(y_test, clf.predict(X_test), digits=3)) ``` **Always inspect the learned features** — this is the step that caught the Hyderabad bug: ```python vec = clf.named_steps["tfidf"] model = clf.named_steps["model"] names = np.array(vec.get_feature_names_out()) coefs = model.coef_[0] order = coefs.argsort() print("MOST NEGATIVE:", list(zip(names[order[:15]], coefs[order[:15]].round(2)))) print("MOST POSITIVE:", list(zip(names[order[-15:]], coefs[order[-15:]].round(2)))) ``` If your top features are `the`, `of`, and `and`, your preprocessing is broken. If they are `terrible`, `waste of`, `not worth`, `refund` — the model has learned something real. **This inspectability is TF-IDF's genuine advantage over embeddings.** You can read exactly why a document was classified as it was, which matters enormously in regulated domains. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Raw text"] --> B["Tokenize"] B --> C["Lowercase +
remove stopwords"] C --> D["Lemmatize"] D --> E["Build vocabulary
unigrams + bigrams"] E --> F["TF-IDF weighting
rare terms ↑"] F --> G["Sparse matrix
(n_docs × n_terms)"] G --> H["Logistic regression"] H --> I["Prediction +
readable feature weights"] ``` ##### Common mistakes - **Using raw counts instead of TF-IDF**, letting boilerplate dominate — 61% versus 87%. - **Removing stopwords for sentiment tasks**, deleting "not," "no," and "never." - **Fitting the vectorizer on train + test**, leaking test vocabulary and IDF statistics. Put it in a `Pipeline`. - **Unigrams only** on tasks where negation or phrases matter. - **No `min_df`**, so typos become features. - **Stemming when lemmatization is affordable** — `univers` conflating university and universe. - **Converting a sparse matrix with `.toarray()`** on a large corpus and exhausting memory. - **Never inspecting the top features.** - **Applying English stopword lists to Hindi or Tamil text.** - **Expecting TF-IDF to understand meaning.** "Great" and "excellent" are entirely unrelated dimensions to it — which is precisely tomorrow's topic. ##### Hands-on: build the classical pipeline once Your practical task is the full preprocessing chain — tokenize, remove stopwords, lemmatize — followed by a TF-IDF sentiment classifier. Print the intermediate output at each stage on one sample document so you can see exactly what each step does. Then run the classifier twice, once with stopwords removed and once without, on sentiment specifically. On many sentiment datasets keeping stopwords actually scores *better*, because negation words survive. Discovering that yourself is worth more than being told. The mini project is a movie-review sentiment analyzer reporting accuracy and top features. The IMDb dataset is the standard choice and is available through `keras.datasets` or Hugging Face. Expect around 88–90% with TF-IDF plus logistic regression — a number worth remembering, because when you build a transformer-based classifier later and get 93%, you will know exactly how much the extra complexity bought. The assignment compares bag-of-words against TF-IDF and explains the difference. Run both with identical settings otherwise, report both scores, and then print the top 20 features from each side by side. The BoW list will be full of function words; the TF-IDF list will be full of content words. That side-by-side table is the explanation — everything else is commentary. ##### Key takeaways - **TF-IDF weights terms by rarity**, which is why it beats raw counts: frequent boilerplate gets zeroed out and discriminative vocabulary rises to the top. - **Preprocessing choices are task-dependent** — stopword removal helps topic classification and can wreck sentiment analysis. - **Bag-of-words discards word order**, making "dog bites man" identical to "man bites dog"; bigrams recover just enough to capture negation. - **Always inspect your top features.** If they are `the` and `of`, your pipeline is broken, and this five-line check catches it instantly. - **TF-IDF has no concept of meaning** — "great" and "excellent" are unrelated dimensions — which is exactly the gap that embeddings fill next.
